blocks.text: Imagine you have a deck of cards and you want to sort them efficiently without using extra space. Heapsort is an algorithm that can do just that by utilizing a data structure called a heap.

blocks.markdown: Heapsort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm that uses a binary heap data structure to sort elements in place. It is particularly useful when you need to sort a large dataset with limited auxiliary space. In this lesson, we will explore how heapsort works, how to construct a heap efficiently, and how it compares with other sorting algorithms like merge sort.

blocks.title: Heap
blocks.text: A heap is a complete binary tree where each parent node is greater than or equal to its child nodes (max-heap) or less than or equal to its child nodes (min-heap).

blocks.markdown: To perform heapsort, we first need to build a max-heap from the input data. Once the max-heap is constructed, the largest element is at the root of the heap. We then repeatedly extract the maximum element and adjust the heap until all elements are sorted.

blocks.title: Building a Max-Heap
blocks.prompt: Given an array [3, 1, 6, 5, 2, 4], build a max-heap.

steps.text: Start with the last non-leaf node, which is at index 2 (value 6).
Check if the children of node 6 need to be swapped. No swap is needed as 6 is already larger than its children.
Move to the next non-leaf node, index 1 (value 1). Swap with the larger child, which is 5.
The array becomes [3, 5, 6, 1, 2, 4]. Now, check node 1 (new value 1) and swap with its larger child 2.
Finally, check the root node, index 0 (value 3). Swap with the larger child 6.

blocks.markdown: The process of building a max-heap can be done in linear time, $O(n)$. This is because the cost of heapifying decreases as we move up the tree, and the number of nodes decreases exponentially.

blocks.title: Bottom-Up Heap Construction
blocks.text: Building a heap from an unsorted array using the bottom-up approach is $O(n)$ due to the reduced work required at higher levels of the tree.

steps.text: Extract the root (maximum element) 6 and swap it with the last element 3.
Reduce the heap size by 1 and heapify the root. The array becomes [5, 3, 4, 2, 1, 6].
Extract the new root 5 and swap with the last element 1.
Repeat the process until the heap size is 1.

blocks.caption: Comparison of Heapsort and Merge Sort

blocks.markdown: Heapsort and merge sort both have a time complexity of $O(n \log n)$, but heapsort has the advantage of requiring only constant space, making it suitable for in-place sorting.

points: Heapsort uses a heap data structure to sort elements in place.
Bottom-up heap construction is efficient with a time complexity of $O(n)$.
Heapsort is space-efficient compared to merge sort.
